items.title: Adoption of the rigid-material model branch: reference mass distribution, rigid placements, orientation and scope
items.statement:
Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following **rigid-material
model** branch, in the spacetime and frames of [[post-cm01-spacetime]] and
[[post-cm01-frames]].

**(i) Reference mass distribution.** A rigid-material model carries, besides
the framework's time and frame structure, a **reference mass distribution**: a
measure $\nu$ on the Borel space $(\mathbb R^3,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^3))$ that
is a mass distribution in the sense of
[[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]] — finite and bounded, with
$\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\overline B_R(0)\bigr)=0$ for some real $R>0$,
and of total mass $m:=\nu(\mathbb R^3)\in(0,+\infty)$ — whose reference
coordinates are **centred**,
$$\int\rho\,d\nu(\rho)=0\in\mathbb R^3 .$$
The label variable $\rho$ is a coordinate of the model's reference placement
and has dimension $\ell$, each component read in metres; the total mass $m$
has dimension $\mu$, read in kilograms, and $R$ has dimension $\ell$ and is
the model's **reference size**
([[def-cm01-units]]). Under the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$,
used only through [[lem-cm-mass-moments-are-finite]] to make the polynomial
moments of $\nu$ of degree at most two finite, the first and second moments
of $\nu$ are finite real numbers. The measure $\nu$ and the number $m$ are
model data: no distribution of mass of any concrete body and no measured mass
is asserted.

**(ii) Time window and motions.** A model carries a **time window**
$I_0\subseteq\mathbb R$, a nondegenerate open interval $(a,b)$ with
$-\infty\le a<b\le+\infty$ and at least two points, read in seconds. Fix an
**inertial frame** of the model, that is the adapted chart
$(o,u,(e_1,e_2,e_3))$ with coordinates $(t,x)$ of [[post-cm01-frames]]. A
**motion** of the model in this frame is a map
$x:I_0\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ for which there exist a map
$c:I_0\to\mathbb R^3$ and a map $R:I_0\to SO(3)$, both of class $C^2$
(componentwise derivatives, [[def-cm-affine-time-space]] for the coordinates
and [[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]] for the target), such that
$$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho\qquad(t\in I_0,\ \rho\in\mathbb R^3).$$
Adopt: the motions of the model are the maps of this form, and the pair
$(c,R)$ is the **configuration path** of the motion. The map
$x(t,\cdot):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ is the **placement** at time $t$ and is
the rigid placement of [[def-cm-rigid-placement-and-body-angular-velocity]]
with translation $c$ and rotation $R$; its material velocity is
$\partial_tx(t,\rho)=c'(t)+R'(t)\rho$, defined by differentiability of $c$ and
of the entries of $R$. The time window $I_0$ is the interval on which the
model's configuration path is considered; the model's time coordinate is
the frame time $t$.

**(iii) Rigidity idealization.** The idealization adopted is that the model
describes a body that does not deform, and its content is the representation
(ii): a placement of the form $x=c+R\rho$ with $R\in SO(3)$ preserves every
mutual distance, since $R(t)$ preserves the Euclidean norm
([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]), so for all $\rho,\rho'\in\mathbb R^3$
the number $\lVert x(t,\rho)-x(t,\rho')\rVert_2=\lVert\rho-\rho'\rVert_2$ is
independent of $t$. The model class (ii) is *adopted* as the definition of a
rigid-material placement; a motion of material points that preserves all
mutual distances but whose label set fails to determine a rotation is not
claimed to be of this form, and the general characterization of
distance-preserving placements is neither asserted nor used on this page.
For a **nondegenerate labeling** — a label set containing the origin and two
linearly independent material vectors — distinct configurations $(c,R)$ and
$(\bar c,\bar R)$ give distinct placements, by [[lem-cm-rigid-labeling-stabilizer]];
the configuration data of (ii) therefore do not overcount for such a body.
Degenerate labelings and degenerate mass distributions are not excluded by
this postulate; the later items of the pair state where invertibility of the
inertial data must be assumed.

**(iv) Centre of mass and orientation.** Because the reference coordinates are
centred, the identity
$$\int x(t,\rho)\,d\nu(\rho)=mc(t)$$
holds for every motion, by linearity of the integral and
$\int\rho\,d\nu=0$; the physical reading is that $c(t)$ is the position of the
centre of mass of the model in the placement at time $t$. The rotation
$R(t)$ is the model's **orientation**: it carries reference coordinates into
the frame's spatial coordinates, and the **body-fixed frame** at time $t$ is
the ordered orthonormal basis $(R(t)e_1,R(t)e_2,R(t)e_3)$ of the spatial
space. The reading of $R(t)$ as the orientation of the placement uses the
nondegeneracy of (iii): for a nondegenerate labeling the material points
determine $R(t)$ uniquely, so the orientation is an attribute of the body's
placement and not of the choice of label coordinates.

**(v) Frame changes.** The description of a motion in a second inertial frame
is obtained by the change of coordinates $t'=t+b$, $x'=Qx+ut+a$ of
[[post-cm01-frames]] clause (iv), applied to every event of the motion; here
$Q\in SO(3)$ and $u\in\mathbb R^3$ are the rotation and the boost velocity of
that clause, written $R$ and $v$ there and renamed here to avoid a clash with
the orientation path $R(t)$ of clause (ii) and with the material velocity
field of the pair's definition. With the same $\rho$ labelling a material
point, the description in the second frame is
$$\tilde x(t',\rho):=Q\,x(t'-b,\rho)+u\,(t'-b)+a .$$
This description is again a motion of the model, with configuration path
$$\tilde c(t')=Qc(t'-b)+u\,(t'-b)+a,\qquad \tilde R(t')=Q\,R(t'-b),$$
because $SO(3)$ is closed under multiplication
([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]); this is a consistency requirement of
the model's frame language, exactly as for the particle worldlines of
[[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (ii). The derived transformation laws of the
angular velocity, of the inertia data and of the kinetic splitting are
theorems of this pair's page, not part of this postulate.

**(vi) No dynamics.** This postulate fixes the kinematic class of the model
and its mass data only. It asserts no force law, no torque law, no equation of
motion for the pair $(c,R)$, and no balance or conservation law; in
particular the model does not by itself constrain the configuration path,
and the effect of forces and torques on a body is a separate model
assumption. It also asserts no measured value of any mass, length, duration
or orientation.

**(vii) Scope and exclusions.** The branch excludes deformation, internal
degrees of freedom such as temperature, chemical state or an independent spin
variable, variable mass, ablation and impact events, contact, friction and
dissipative constitutive laws, and any relativistic or quantum description.
It excludes bodies whose mass distribution is not a bounded finite Borel
measure of the stated kind. A rigid-material model is not a system of
finitely many particle labels: the continuum measure $\nu$ carries the mass
data of the model, and the situations of point masses are the special cases
of measures supported on finitely many points. All physical statements about
the model weight material points by $\nu$; properties of $\nu$-null sets of
labels are not physical properties of the body.
items.physical_scope: Adoption of the rigid-material model branch of the framework: a bounded finite Borel measure (the reference mass distribution) of positive total mass with reference coordinates centred at its first moment, a nondegenerate time window, and motions given by rigid placements $x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with $C^{2}$ translation and rotation curves into $SO(3)$. The idealization adopted is kinematic rigidity: all material mutual distances are constant in time. The branch excludes deformation, internal degrees of freedom, variable mass, impacts, and every force, torque, equation of motion, balance or conservation law for the configuration path; it asserts no measured mass, length, duration or orientation and no claim that any concrete body is rigid. It is a declared model branch distinct from the finitely many particle labels of the particle branch.

items.title: Configuration, configuration space and orientation of a rigid-material model in an inertial frame
items.statement:
Adopt the model data, the time window $I_0$, the inertial frame and the
notation of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: the reference mass distribution
$\nu$ with total mass $m$ and centred reference coordinates, and a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with configuration path $(c,R)$ of class $C^2$.

**(a) Configuration and configuration space.** The **configuration** of the
model at time $t$ in the frame is the pair $(c(t),R(t))$; the pair
$(c,R)$ is a **configuration path**. The **configuration space** of the model
is the set
$$\mathcal C:=\mathbb R^3\times SO(3),$$
read through the identification of $M_3(\mathbb R)$ with $\mathbb R^{9}$
([[def-matrix-space]]) so that $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathbb R^{12}$. The
configuration determines the placement $x=c+R\,\cdot$ at that time, and the
reference placement is $(c,R)=(0,I_3)$. Under the identification of
$M_3(\mathbb R)$ with $\mathbb R^{9}$, the group $SO(3)$ is a compact
three-dimensional embedded submanifold of $M_3(\mathbb R)$ and a subgroup of
the general linear group ([[lem-cm-so3-is-a-compact-three-dimensional-embedded-submanifold]]
clauses 1 and 3, [[lem-cm-so3-is-a-matrix-group]]); consequently
$\mathcal C=\mathbb R^3\times SO(3)$ is a six-dimensional smooth manifold
with the product structure. Its dimension $3+3=6$ is read as three
translation coordinates of $c$ and three orientation degrees of freedom of
$R$; the model of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]] has no other configuration
degrees of freedom, since deformation and internal variables are excluded by
that postulate.

**(b) Centre of mass, orientation, body frame.** Because
$\int\rho\,d\nu=0$, the configuration's translation is the position of the
centre of mass of the model,
$\int x(t,\rho)\,d\nu(\rho)=mc(t)$. The rotation $R(t)$ is the **orientation**
of the model at time $t$: the linear map that carries reference coordinates
into the frame's spatial coordinates, so that a material point whose
reference coordinate is $\rho$ is found at the spatial position $x(t,\rho)$.
The **body-fixed frame** at time $t$ is the ordered orthonormal basis
$(R(t)e_1,R(t)e_2,R(t)e_3)$ of the spatial space, obtained by applying the
orientation to the standard basis; the basis is $g$-orthonormal because
$R(t)\in O(3)$ preserves the Euclidean inner product
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]). The
material point of reference coordinate $\rho$ has **spatial position**
$x(t,\rho)$ and **reference coordinates** $\rho$.

**(c) Faithfulness for nondegenerate labelings.** Suppose the label set
$S\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ contains the origin and two linearly independent
material vectors, and let $(c,R)$ and $(\bar c,\bar R)$ be configurations with
$c+R\rho=\bar c+\bar R\rho$ for every $\rho\in S$. Evaluating at the origin of
$S$ gives $c=\bar c$; then $\bar R^{-1}R$ is an element of $SO(3)$ fixing every
vector of $S$, so $\bar R^{-1}R=I_3$ by [[lem-cm-rigid-labeling-stabilizer]]
and $R=\bar R$.
Hence for a nondegenerate labeling the assignment
$(c,R)\mapsto(x:=c+R\,\cdot)$ is injective on configurations, and the
orientation and the centre-of-mass position are attributes of the placement
rather than artefacts of the parametrization. For a labeling supported on a line through
the origin, by contrast, the rotations about that line fix the labels and the
placement determines $R$ only up to composition with them; such a labeling is
called **degenerate** and its orientation contains data not visible in the
placed material points. Both cases are configurations of the model; the
distinction is recorded here because later items use it.

**(d) Description in another inertial frame.** Let a second inertial frame be
related to the first by the transformation $t'=t+b$, $x'=Qx+ut+a$ of
[[post-cm01-frames]] clause (iv), with $b\in\mathbb R$, $a,u\in\mathbb R^3$
and $Q\in SO(3)$
([[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]] clause 1); the letters
$Q$ and $u$ are the rotation and the boost velocity written $R$ and $v$ in
[[post-cm01-frames]], renamed to avoid clashes with the orientation path
$R(t)$ and the material velocity field of clause (e). The
**description of the same motion in the second frame** assigns to the same
material label $\rho$ the events of the motion in the new coordinates,
$$\tilde x(t',\rho):=Q\,x(t'-b,\rho)+u\,(t'-b)+a .$$
Substituting $x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ and using distributivity of the matrix
product over sums expresses the description as a motion of the same model in
the second frame, with configuration path
$$\tilde c(t')=Qc(t'-b)+u\,(t'-b)+a,\qquad \tilde R(t')=Q\,R(t'-b),$$
where $\tilde R(t')\in SO(3)$ for every $t'$ because $SO(3)$ is closed under
matrix multiplication ([[lem-cm-so3-is-a-matrix-group]]); the pair
$(\tilde c,\tilde R)$ is again of class $C^2$. This description is a
convention forced by the frame change,
not a dynamical statement; the transformation laws of the velocity field, the
angular velocity and the inertia data are proved in the frame-covariance
theorem of this page.

**(e) Material velocities.** For a motion with configuration path $(c,R)$, the
**material velocity** of the label $\rho$ at time $t$ is the derivative
$$\partial_tx(t,\rho):=c'(t)+R'(t)\rho,$$
which exists by differentiability of $c$ and of the entries of $R$
([[def-cm-rigid-placement-and-body-angular-velocity]]). The **velocity field
of the motion** at time $t$ is the map
$p\mapsto v(t,p)$ assigning to a spatial point the velocity of the material
point currently placed there, defined on the image of the placement. Neither
the configuration nor the placement by itself asserts a dynamics: the pair
$(c,R)$ is a description of the position and orientation of the body, and the
material velocity is its kinematic derivative.
items.strategy: A definition: it fixes the configuration pair (c,R) of the rigid-material model, the configuration space R^3 x SO(3) with its manifold structure and dimension six, the centre-of-mass and orientation readings, the body-fixed frame, the faithfulness of the parametrization for nondegenerate labelings and the description of the same motion in a second inertial frame.
items.physical_scope: The configuration data of the rigid-material model branch of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]] in one fixed inertial frame: the configuration pair (c,R) of centre-of-mass position and orientation, its reading as a placement of the reference mass distribution, the configuration space $\mathbb R^3\times SO(3)$ with the dimension three plus three, the body-fixed orthonormal frame, the reference placement, the faithfulness of the parametrization for nondegenerate labelings, and the description of the same motion in a second inertial frame. No force, torque, equation of motion, time evolution or measured value is asserted.

items.title: Body and spatial angular velocity of a rigid-material motion, and the material velocity field
items.statement:
Adopt the model, inertial frame and notation of
[[post-cm10-rigid-material]] and [[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]], and
let a motion $x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ have configuration path $(c,R)$ of
class $C^2$ on the time window $I_0$ ([[def-interval]]).

**(a) Body angular velocity.** By
[[def-cm-rigid-placement-and-body-angular-velocity]], the matrix
$R(t)^{\mathsf T}R'(t)$ is skew-symmetric at every $t\in I_0$
([[lem-cm-matrix-curve-derivative-rules]] clause 3), and by
[[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]] clause 2 there is exactly
one vector $\omega(t)\in\mathbb R^3$ with
$$R(t)^{\mathsf T}R'(t)=[\omega(t)]_\times .$$
The map $\omega:I_0\to\mathbb R^3$ is the **body angular velocity** of the
motion. Since $R$ is of class $C^2$, the entries of $R^{\mathsf T}R'$ are
differentiable and hence $\omega$ is of class $C^1$; its derivative is the
**body angular acceleration**. The dimension is $[\omega]=\tau^{-1}$
([[def-cm01-units]]), read in radians per second under the radian convention,
in which angles are dimensionless.

**(b) Spatial angular velocity.** The **spatial angular velocity** of the
motion is
$$\omega_{\mathrm s}(t):=R(t)\omega(t)\in\mathbb R^3,$$
of the same dimension $\tau^{-1}$. By the conjugation clause of
[[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]],
$R'(t)R(t)^{\mathsf T}=[\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)]_\times$; this is the
space-frame rate matrix of the motion.

**(c) Material velocity field.** For every material label $\rho$,
$$\partial_tx(t,\rho)=c'(t)+R(t)\bigl(\omega(t)\times\rho\bigr),$$
because $R'(t)=R(t)[\omega(t)]_\times$ and
$[\omega]_\times\rho=\omega\times\rho$
([[def-cm-rigid-placement-and-body-angular-velocity]],
[[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]] clause 1). Writing
$p=x(t,\rho)$ for the spatial position of the label and using
$R(\omega\times\rho)=(R\omega)\times(R\rho)$, the same identity reads
$$\partial_tx(t,\rho)=c'(t)+\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)\times\bigl(p-c(t)\bigr):$$
the material velocity field is that of a translation $c'(t)$ composed with a
rotation of angular velocity $\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$ about the centre of mass
$c(t)$. The motion is a **pure translation** at time $t$ exactly when
$\omega(t)=0$, equivalently $R'(t)=0$; then every material velocity equals
$c'(t)$.

**(d) Uniqueness of the velocity data.** The velocity field determines
$c'(t)$ and $\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$ uniquely: if a motion has material
velocity field $p\mapsto v(t,p)=c'(t)+\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)\times(p-c(t))$,
then evaluating at $p=c(t)$ gives $c'(t)=v(t,c(t))$, and for $u\in\mathbb R^3$
the difference $v(t,c(t)+u)-v(t,c(t))=\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)\times u$ is a
linear map of $u$; testing it on two linearly independent vectors determines
$\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$ by the injectivity clause of
[[lem-cm-skew-matrix-cross-product-correspondence]], and then
$\omega(t)=R(t)^{\mathsf T}\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$. The pair
$\bigl(c'(t),\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)\bigr)$ is therefore an intrinsic
description of the velocity field; the body angular velocity is its
description in the body-fixed frame, and the choice of reference coordinates
is part of the model data fixed in [[post-cm10-rigid-material]].

**(e) Instantaneous rotation axis.** If $\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)\neq0$, the line
$$\bigl\{c(t)+s\,\omega_{\mathrm s}(t):s\in\mathbb R\bigr\}$$
is the **instantaneous rotation axis** of the motion at time $t$: it is the
set of spatial points whose material velocity equals $c'(t)$, as follows from
$\omega_{\mathrm s}\times(\omega_{\mathrm s}s)=0$. The velocity field is
constant on lines parallel to $\omega_{\mathrm s}(t)$ and rotates about this
axis; if also $c'(t)=0$ at that instant, every point of the axis is
instantaneously at rest and the motion is an instantaneous rotation about it.
No claim is made that the axis is fixed in time or in space.

**(f) Conventions and scope.** The convention fixed here is the body-fixed
one of the cited mathematical definition: $\Omega=R^{\mathsf T}R'=[\omega]_\times$
and $R'=R\Omega$. A consumer using the space-fixed convention must state the
change, which is the rotation by $R$ recorded in (b); the two vectors agree
only when $R(t)$ fixes $\omega(t)$. Both vectors are kinematic quantities of
the motion: no torque, no angular momentum and no equation of motion for
$\omega$ is asserted, and no measured angular velocity is recorded. The
behaviour of $\omega$ under a change of inertial frame is proved in the
frame-covariance theorem of this page.
items.strategy: A definition: it fixes the body angular velocity by R^T R' = [omega]_x, the spatial angular velocity, the spatial form of the material velocity field, the uniqueness of the velocity data, the instantaneous rotation axis and the convention, with dimension tau^{-1}.
items.physical_scope: The angular velocity of the rigid-material model branch of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]] along a $C^{2}$ motion in one inertial frame: the body angular velocity $\omega$ characterised by $R^{\mathsf T}R'=[\omega]_\times$, the spatial angular velocity $\omega_{\mathrm{s}}=R\omega$, the spatial form of the material velocity field and its uniqueness, and the instantaneous rotation axis when $\omega_{\mathrm{s}}\neq0$, with the dimension $\tau^{-1}$ read in radians per second under the radian convention. The item is kinematic: it asserts no torque, no equation of motion for $\omega$ and no measured value.

items.title: Inertia matrix, spatial inertia tensor, inertia tensor about a point and moment of inertia about an axis of a rigid-material model
items.statement:
Adopt the model of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: the reference mass
distribution $\nu$, its total mass $m=\nu(\mathbb R^3)$ and its centred
reference coordinates $\int\rho\,d\nu(\rho)=0$. Assume the Axiom of Countable
Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, used only through
[[lem-cm-mass-moments-are-finite]] to make the polynomial moments of $\nu$ of
degree at most two finite real numbers. Fix an inertial frame and a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with configuration path $(c,R)$ of class $C^2$
([[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]]).

**(a) Body inertia matrix.** The **body inertia matrix** of the model is the
inertia matrix of the reference mass distribution,
$$I:=I(\nu)=\int\bigl(\lVert\rho\rVert_2^{2}I_3-\rho\rho^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho)\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
with entries $I_{jk}=\int(\lVert\rho\rVert_2^{2}\delta_{jk}-\rho_j\rho_k)\,d\nu$
as in [[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]]; the matrix is expressed
in the standard basis of the reference coordinates. Its entries are finite
real numbers, it is symmetric, and for every $\omega\in\mathbb R^3$,
$$\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\int\lVert\omega\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho)\ \ge 0$$
by [[lem-cm-inertia-matrix-properties]] clauses 1-2; hence $I$ is symmetric
and its quadratic form is positive semidefinite. The dimension is
$[I]=\mu\ell^{2}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]), read in kilogram metres squared. The
model is **nondegenerate** when no line through the origin carries the whole
mass, that is $\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb R\omega\bigr)>0$ for every
$\omega\neq0$, and **degenerate** otherwise; the connection between this
criterion and the strict positivity and invertibility of $I$ is proved in the
principal-axes theorem of this page.

**(b) Spatial inertia tensor at the centre of mass.** The **spatial inertia
tensor** of the model at time $t$ is
$$I(t):=R(t)\,I\,R(t)^{\mathsf T}\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
the matrix of the same quadratic form in the frame's spatial coordinates: for
every $n\in\mathbb R^3$,
$n^{\mathsf T}I(t)n=(R(t)^{\mathsf T}n)^{\mathsf T}I(R(t)^{\mathsf T}n)$. Its
entries are $C^2$ functions of $t$, since $R$ is of class $C^2$ and $I$ is
constant; the matrix rotates with the body and returns to $I$ in the
body-fixed frame, where $R=I_3$.

**(c) Inertia tensor about a spatial point.** For a spatial point
$p\in\mathbb R^3$ let
$$a(t,p):=R(t)^{\mathsf T}\bigl(p-c(t)\bigr)\in\mathbb R^3$$
be the **reference coordinate of $p$**, that is the label of the material
point of the reference placement that is placed at $p$ at time $t$. The
**inertia tensor of the model about $p$** at time $t$ is
$$I(t,p):=R(t)\,I_\nu\bigl(a(t,p)\bigr)\,R(t)^{\mathsf T}\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$
where
$$I_\nu(a)=\int\bigl(\lVert\rho-a\rVert_2^{2}I_3-(\rho-a)(\rho-a)^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho)$$
is the inertia tensor of the mass distribution about the point $a$ of the
reference coordinates ([[def-cm-inertia-tensor-about-a-point]]). Since the
label of a spatial point is uniquely determined by the placement, this is
well defined; for the centre of mass, $a(t,c(t))=0$ and
$I(t,c(t))=I(t)$. The dimension is again $\mu\ell^{2}$, read in kilogram
metres squared.

**(d) Moment of inertia about an axis.** Let $\ell$ be a spatial line at time
$t$, given by a point $p\in\mathbb R^3$ and a unit direction $n\in\mathbb R^3$
($\lVert n\rVert_2=1$). The **moment of inertia of the model about $\ell$** is
$$\Theta_\ell(t):=n^{\mathsf T}I(t,p)n .$$
Its invariance under the choices entering the description of the line and
its identification with the integral defining the physical moment of inertia
about the line are statements, not conventions; they are proved in clause
(c) of the principal-axes theorem of this page. For a **body-fixed
axis**, that is a line through the centre of mass whose direction in
reference coordinates is a constant unit vector $n_0$, the moment is
$$n_0^{\mathsf T}I n_0=\int\lVert n_0\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho),$$
by clause (a), and is independent of time, because $I$ and $n_0$ are model
data.

**(e) What is constant and what moves.** The body inertia matrix $I$ is
determined by the model's reference mass distribution alone and does not
depend on the time, the frame or the motion; the spatial inertia tensor
$I(t)$ depends on the motion through the orientation $R(t)$; the inertia
tensor $I(t,p)$ about a spatial point depends on the motion through both the
orientation and the position of $p$. Principal axes and principal moments of
$I$ are the subject of the principal-axes theorem of this page.
items.strategy: A definition: it fixes the body inertia matrix, the spatial inertia tensor, the inertia tensor about a spatial point, the moment of inertia about an axis and the nondegeneracy naming, with dimension mu l^2 and the cited mathematical properties.
items.physical_scope: The inertia data of the rigid-material model branch of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: the body inertia matrix of the reference mass distribution about the centre of mass, its spatial version along a motion, the inertia tensor of the model about an arbitrary spatial point, and the moment of inertia about an axis, with the dimension $\mu\ell^{2}$ read in kilogram metres squared. The item states the mathematical properties it uses (symmetry, positivity and the nondegeneracy criterion) through their cited mathematical suppliers. No measured inertia is asserted and no rotational dynamics is introduced.

items.title: Total momentum, kinetic-energy splitting and centre-of-mass angular momentum of a rigid-material motion
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), used only to make the integrals below finite.
Adopt the model and notation of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: a reference
mass distribution $\nu$ with total mass $m$ and centred reference coordinates,
a fixed inertial frame, and a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ with configuration path $(c,R)$ of class $C^{2}$ on
the time window $I_0$, body angular velocity $\omega$
([[def-cm10-angular-velocity]]) and body inertia matrix $I$
([[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]]). Define the **total momentum**, **kinetic
energy** and **angular momentum about the centre of mass** of the model along
the motion by the componentwise integrals
$$P(t):=\int\partial_tx(t,\rho)\,d\nu(\rho),\qquad K(t):=\frac12\int\lVert\partial_tx(t,\rho)\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho),$$
$$L_c(t):=\int\bigl(x(t,\rho)-c(t)\bigr)\times\bigl(\partial_tx(t,\rho)-c'(t)\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho),$$
with dimensions $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$, $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ and
$\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]). Then for every $t\in I_0$:

1. the three integrands are $\nu$-integrable, so $P(t)$, $K(t)$ and
   $L_c(t)$ are a well-defined finite vector and finite real numbers;
2. $P(t)=m\,c'(t)$;
3. $K(t)=\dfrac12m\lVert c'(t)\rVert_2^{2}+\dfrac12\omega(t)^{\mathsf T}I\omega(t)$;
4. $L_c(t)=R(t)\,I\,\omega(t)$.

The identities hold for every $C^{2}$ configuration path; no equation of
motion, force law or conservation statement is used or asserted.
items.physical_scope: Conditional inertial identities of the rigid-material model branch of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]] along a $C^{2}$ motion in one inertial frame: the total momentum equals the total mass times the centre-of-mass velocity; the kinetic energy splits into the centre-of-mass term and the rotational term $\tfrac12\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega$; and the angular momentum about the centre of mass equals $RI\omega$. The statements are identities for the model's measure, motion and inertia data, under the countable-choice assumption used only for the finiteness of the integrals. No conservation law, no force law and no measured value is asserted.

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, January 2015 printing), Section 3.2.2, Eqs. K. K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Part CM: Classical Mechanics (title page last edited September 1, 2026), Chapter 4 Section 4.2, Eqs. (4.14)-(4.22), chapter pages 4-6 (PDF pages 58-60): rotational kinetic energy through the inertia tensor and the angular momentum $\mathbf L=I\boldsymbol\omega$

G. J. Sussman and J. Wisdom, Structure and Interpretation of Classical Mechanics, 2nd ed. (MIT Press, 2014), Section 2.1, Eq. (2.10), and Section 2.6, Eq. (2.51): the kinetic-energy split for a rigid body and the vector angular momentum through the inertia tensor

items.title: Principal axes and principal moments of the inertia data of a rigid-material model, axis moments and extremal values
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), used only to make the integrals finite. Adopt the
model of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]] and its inertia data
([[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]]): the reference mass distribution $\nu$ with
total mass $m$ and centred reference coordinates, the body inertia matrix $I$,
the spatial inertia tensor $I(t)=R(t)IR(t)^{\mathsf T}$ of a motion
$x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$, and the inertia tensor $I(t,p)$ about a spatial
point $p$ ([[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]]). Then:

**(a) Principal basis.** There is an orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of
$\mathbb R^3$ and real numbers $I_1,I_2,I_3$, the **principal axes** and
**principal moments** of the model, with
$$Ie_j=I_je_j\qquad(j=1,2,3).$$

**(b) Quadratic form and rotational term.** For every
$\omega=\sum_j\omega_je_j\in\mathbb R^3$ one has
$I\omega=\sum_jI_j\omega_je_j$ and
$$\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\sum_jI_j\omega_j^{2}=\int\lVert\omega\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho)\ \ge 0,$$
and each principal moment is
$I_j=e_j^{\mathsf T}Ie_j=\int\lVert e_j\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho)$.

**(c) Axis moments.** For every unit vector $n\in\mathbb R^3$,
$$n^{\mathsf T}In=\int\lVert n\times\rho\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho);$$
for every spatial point $p$ and unit vector $n$, with $x=x(t,\cdot)$ the
placement at time $t$,
$$n^{\mathsf T}I(t,p)n=\int\lVert n\times\bigl(x(t,\rho)-p\bigr)\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho).$$
Consequently the number $\Theta_\ell(t)=n^{\mathsf T}I(t,p)n$ of
[[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]] depends only on the spatial line $\ell$
$\{p+sn:s\in\mathbb R\}$ and not on the choice of the point $p$ on it nor on
the sign of the unit direction $n$.

**(d) Vanishing and positivity.** Each principal moment satisfies $I_j\ge0$,
and $I_j=0$ exactly when $\nu$ is supported on the line $\mathbb Re_j$ of the
principal axis, that is $\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb Re_j\bigr)=0$.
If the model is nondegenerate, that is if
$\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\mathbb R\omega\bigr)>0$ for every
$\omega\neq0$, then every $I_j>0$ and $I$ is invertible. If $\nu$ is
supported on some line through the origin (such a line exists whenever the
support of a centred $\nu$ is contained in a line, because the mean of $\nu$
is the origin), then $I$ is not invertible.

**(e) Extremal moments.** For every unit vector
$n=\sum_jc_je_j$ one has $n^{\mathsf T}In=\sum_jI_jc_j^{2}$ and therefore
$$\min_jI_j\ \le\ n^{\mathsf T}In\ \le\ \max_jI_j,$$
with the value $\max_jI_j$ attained at a unit eigenvector for a maximal
principal moment and the value $\min_jI_j$ attained at a unit eigenvector for
a minimal principal moment. Hence the largest and smallest principal moments
are the maximum and minimum of the rotational-inertia quadratic form over the
unit sphere.

The identities are conditional on the model data and the stated choice
assumption; no equation of motion and no conservation statement is used or
asserted.
items.physical_scope: The principal-axis structure of the inertia data of the rigid-material model branch of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: existence of an orthonormal principal basis with real principal moments, the identification of the quadratic form with the moment of inertia about an axis (body-fixed and spatial versions), the vanishing and positivity criteria for degenerate and nondegenerate mass distributions, and the extremal character of the largest and smallest principal moments. The identities are conditional on the model data and the countable-choice assumption used only for finiteness of the integrals. No measured inertia, no dynamics and no claim about any concrete body is asserted.

G. J. Sussman and J. Wisdom, Structure and Interpretation of Classical Mechanics, 2nd ed. (MIT Press, 2014), Section 2.5: the principal moments as the eigenvalues of the inertia tensor and the diagonal form in the principal basis

items.title: Behaviour of the rigid-material configuration, angular velocity, inertia data and inertial quantities under a change of inertial frame
items.statement:
Adopt the model of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]] and notation of
[[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]], [[def-cm10-angular-velocity]] and
[[def-cm10-inertia-tensor]]: a reference mass distribution $\nu$ with total
mass $m$ and centred reference coordinates, a body inertia matrix $I$, a
motion $x(t,\rho)=c(t)+R(t)\rho$ in one inertial frame with configuration path
$(c,R)$ of class $C^2$ and body angular velocity $\omega$, and the quantities
of [[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]],
$$P(t)=\int\partial_tx(t,\rho)\,d\nu(\rho),\qquad K(t)=\frac12\int\lVert\partial_tx(t,\rho)\rVert_2^{2}\,d\nu(\rho),\qquad L_c(t)=\int\bigl(x(t,\rho)-c(t)\bigr)\times\bigl(\partial_tx(t,\rho)-c'(t)\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho).$$
Let a second inertial frame be related to the first by the transformation
$t'=t+b$, $x'=Qx+ut+a$ of [[post-cm01-frames]] clause (iv), with
$b\in\mathbb R$, $a,u\in\mathbb R^3$ and $Q\in SO(3)$; the rotation $Q$ and
the boost velocity $u$ are the parameters written $R$ and $v$ in
[[post-cm01-frames]], renamed here to avoid clashes with the orientation path
$R(t)$ and the material velocity field $v(t,p)$ of
[[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]]. Let
$\tilde x(t',\rho):=Q\,x(t'-b,\rho)+u\,(t'-b)+a$ be the description of the
same motion in the second frame. Then:

1. $\tilde x(t',\rho)=\tilde c(t')+\tilde R(t')\rho$ with
   $\tilde c(t')=Qc(t'-b)+u\,(t'-b)+a$ and
   $\tilde R(t')=Q\,R(t'-b)$; the maps $\tilde c$ and $\tilde R$ are of class
   $C^2$, $\tilde R$ takes values in $SO(3)$, and $\tilde x$ is a motion of
   the same model with the same reference mass distribution;
2. the body angular velocities satisfy
   $\tilde\omega(t')=\omega(t'-b)$, and the spatial angular velocities satisfy
   $\tilde\omega_{\mathrm s}(t')=Q\omega_{\mathrm s}(t'-b)$;
3. the material velocity fields satisfy
   $\partial_{t'}\tilde x(t',\rho)=Q\,\partial_tx(t'-b,\rho)+u$;
   equivalently, for a spatial point $p$ of the first frame with image
   $p'=Qp+ut+a$, $\tilde v(t',p')=Q\,v(t,p)+u$;
4. the body inertia matrix computed from $\nu$ is the same matrix $I$ in
   either frame, and the spatial inertia tensors satisfy
   $\tilde I(t')=Q\,I(t'-b)\,Q^{\mathsf T}$; consequently
   $\tilde\omega(t')^{\mathsf T}I\tilde\omega(t')=\omega(t'-b)^{\mathsf T}I\omega(t'-b)$
   and
   $\tilde\omega_{\mathrm s}(t')^{\mathsf T}\tilde I(t')\tilde\omega_{\mathrm s}(t')=\omega_{\mathrm s}(t'-b)^{\mathsf T}I(t'-b)\omega_{\mathrm s}(t'-b)$;
5. the inertial quantities satisfy
   $$\tilde P(t')=Q\,P(t'-b)+mu,\qquad \tilde L_c(t')=Q\,L_c(t'-b),$$
   $$\tilde K(t')=\frac12m\lVert Qc'(t'-b)+u\rVert_2^{2}+\frac12\omega(t'-b)^{\mathsf T}I\omega(t'-b).$$

The statements are kinematic and inertial identities for the model; no
equation of motion, no conservation law and no measured value is asserted.
items.physical_scope: Transformation laws of the rigid-material model branch of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]] between two inertial frames related by $t'=t+b$, $x'=Qx+ut+a$: the configuration path and material velocity field of the same motion in the new frame, invariance of the body angular velocity and rotation of the spatial angular velocity and of the spatial inertia tensor, and the transformation of the total momentum, kinetic-energy splitting and centre-of-mass angular momentum. The statements are conditional kinematic and inertial identities for the model; no dynamics and no measured value is asserted.

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, January 2015 printing), Section 3.1.2, printed pages 49-50 (PDF pages 55-56): the parallel discussion of body and space angular-velocity descriptions and the convention-dependence of the extracted vector

K. K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Part CM: Classical Mechanics (title page last edited September 1, 2026), Chapter 4 Sections 4.1-4.2, Eqs. (4.1)-(4.22), chapter pages 1-6 (PDF pages 55-60): moving-basis kinematics and the inertia data of the moving frame

G. J. Sussman and J. Wisdom, Structure and Interpretation of Classical Mechanics, 2nd ed. (MIT Press, 2014), Section 2.2: the body-frame description of the same rigid motion and the transformation between body and space quantities

items.title: The global orientation and its charts: Euler angles, the quaternion double cover and singularities of parametrizations
items.statement:
For the model of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]], the orientation of the body at
time $t$ is the element $R(t)\in SO(3)$ of the configuration
([[def-cm10-rigid-body-configuration]]): a global object attached to the
placement, unique for a nondegenerate labeling. As a subset of
$M_3(\mathbb R)\cong\mathbb R^9$, the group $SO(3)$ is a compact
three-dimensional embedded submanifold and a matrix group
([[lem-cm-so3-is-a-compact-three-dimensional-embedded-submanifold]] clauses
1 and 3, [[lem-cm-so3-is-a-matrix-group]]). Three descriptions of it are used
in the literature and on the pages that follow, and they must not be
conflated.

**Euler angles are local coordinates.** The Euler-angle parametrization of
[[def-cm-euler-angle-parametrization-and-heavy-top-system]] is
$$\Theta:\mathbb R\times(0,\pi)\times\mathbb R\longrightarrow SO(3),\qquad \Theta(\varphi,\theta,\psi)=R_z(\varphi)R_y(\theta)R_z(\psi),$$
with the coordinate rotation matrices of
[[lem-cm-coordinate-rotation-matrices]], and its domain is deliberately
restricted to $\theta\in(0,\pi)$ so that $\sin\theta>0$. On that domain it is
a local chart; the boundary values $\theta=0$ and $\theta=\pi$ (the **poles**)
are excluded because there the dependence on the angles collapses: by the
composition law $R_z(a)R_z(b)=R_z(a+b)$ the value at $\theta=0$ depends on
$\varphi+\psi$ alone. A smooth orientation path of the model can pass through
a pole orientation — the identity $I_3$ is such a point — while no single
continuous choice of the three angles through that point exists; the
companion page's example on the Euler-angle pole exhibits the failure of
injectivity and of invertibility of the derivative there. Euler angles are
therefore a local, singular coordinate device, not a
description of the orientation itself. The angular-velocity components are
not the coordinate derivatives of these angles
([[lem-cm-euler-angle-angular-velocity]] is the separate relation, and the
model's angular velocity is defined intrinsically in
[[def-cm10-angular-velocity]]).

**Quaternion lifts are two-valued, not a single-valued chart.** Under the
countable choice hypothesis recorded in
[[def-cm-quaternion-rotation-map-and-cover]], the unit quaternions $S^3$
double-cover $SO(3)$ through the rotation map $\rho$: every orientation has
exactly two preimages $q$ and $-q$. Given a $C^1$ rotation path $R$ and an
initial unit quaternion $q_0$ with $\rho(q_0)=R(t_0)$, there is exactly one
$C^1$ lift $q$ with $q(t_0)=q_0$, and every $C^1$ lift is either $q$ or $-q$
([[thm-cm-quaternion-lift-exists-and-is-unique]]). The sign of a lift is thus
an initial choice that the orientation path itself does not determine, and no
construction on these pages chooses a preferred sign. A quaternion path is a
global description of a rotation path in the sense that it avoids the Euler
pole, but it represents each orientation twice; it is not a chart of $SO(3)$
and does not select a canonical sign.
items.strategy: A scope remark: it audits the orientation description of the model (global R in SO(3) versus Euler-angle charts with poles and quaternion lifts with a sign choice), records the conventions consumers must state, the degenerate-labeling caveat and the empirical status.
items.physical_scope: Scope and interpretation of the orientation data of the rigid-material model branch of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: the physical orientation is the global element $R\in SO(3)$ of the configuration, while Euler angles are local coordinates with poles and quaternion lifts are global two-valued representations whose sign is an initial choice. The item records the singularities and the bookkeeping conventions of these descriptions and their physical reading; it asserts no dynamics, no measured orientation and no preferred chart.

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, January 2015 printing), Section 3.5, printed pages 62-65 (PDF pages 68-71): the three ordered rotations defining the Euler angles, the caution about the order and frame conventions, and the local character of the parametrization

K. K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Part CM: Classical Mechanics (title page last edited September 1, 2026), Chapter 4 Section 4.5, Eqs. (4.70)-(4.82), chapter pages 15-19 (PDF pages 69-73): Euler angles as local coordinates of the rigid-body configuration, with the general warning that the angular-velocity components are not coordinate derivatives

G. J. Sussman and J. Wisdom, Structure and Interpretation of Classical Mechanics, 2nd ed. (MIT Press, 2014), Section 2.7 and Section 2.12: Euler-angle charts, their singular character at the poles, and quaternions as an alternative global description of orientation

items.title: An equilateral-triangle rigid-material model: inertia matrix, principal axes, rotational term and the threefold-symmetry check
items.statement:
Adopt a rigid-material model of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]] whose reference
mass distribution is the finite weighted sum of Dirac measures
$$\nu:=m_0\delta_{x_1}+m_0\delta_{x_2}+m_0\delta_{x_3},\qquad x_k:=a\Bigl(\cos\frac{2\pi k}{3},\ \sin\frac{2\pi k}{3},\ 0\Bigr)\quad(k=0,1,2),$$
with equal weights $m_0>0$ and circumradius $a>0$; the parameters are model
data, not measurements. Then:

1. $\nu$ is a centred mass distribution of total mass $m=3m_0$ in the sense
   of [[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]];
2. the body inertia matrix is
   $$I=\mathrm{diag}\Bigl(\frac{3m_0a^{2}}{2},\ \frac{3m_0a^{2}}{2},\ 3m_0a^{2}\Bigr);$$
3. the principal axes are $e_3$ together with any $g$-orthonormal pair in the
   plane $e_3=0$, and the principal moments are $\frac{3m_0a^{2}}{2}$ (twice)
   and $3m_0a^{2}$; the model is nondegenerate and $I$ is invertible;
4. for any motion of the model with body angular velocity
   $\omega=\sum_j\omega_je_j$, the rotational term of
   [[pthm-cm10-kinetic-splitting]] is
   $$\frac12\omega^{\mathsf T}I\omega=\frac12\cdot\frac{3m_0a^{2}}{2}\bigl(\omega_1^{2}+\omega_2^{2}\bigr)+\frac12\cdot3m_0a^{2}\omega_3^{2};$$
5. the threefold rotation $S:=R_z(2\pi/3)$ satisfies $SI S^{\mathsf T}=I$, so
   the inertia data of the equilateral triangle are invariant under the
   symmetry rotation of the shape, and the two equal transverse principal
   moments are its trace.
items.physical_scope: A worked rigid-material model: three equal point masses at the vertices of an equilateral triangle in reference coordinates centred at the triangle's centre. The example computes the model's body inertia matrix, its principal axes and moments, the rotational term of the kinetic splitting for a general motion, and the invariance of the inertia matrix under the threefold symmetry rotation. It is a model instance with declared numerical proportions of the parameters; no measured moment of inertia and no concrete physical body is asserted.

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, January 2015 printing), Section 3.2, Eqs. (3.19)-(3.23), printed pages 50-52 (PDF pages 56-58): inertia tensors of finite point-mass systems, principal axes and the semidefiniteness discussion

K. K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Part CM: Classical Mechanics (title page last edited September 1, 2026), Chapter 4 Section 4.2, Eqs. (4.14)-(4.22), chapter pages 4-6 (PDF pages 58-60): computed inertia tensors of discrete mass distributions and the rotational kinetic energy
G. J. Sussman and J. Wisdom, Structure and Interpretation of Classical Mechanics, 2nd ed. (MIT Press, 2014), Sections 2.3-2.5: moments of inertia and principal moments of discrete mass distributions

items.title: A rigid-material model of two point masses on a line: the inertia matrix can be singular, and rotation about the line is invisible to the rotational term
items.statement:
In the rigid-material model branch of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]], **every
model of positive total mass has a positive definite inertia matrix**:
equivalently, every principal moment of the body inertia matrix $I$ is
strictly positive and $I$ is invertible.
items.physical_scope: A counterexample inside the rigid-material model branch of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: two equal point masses at opposite points of a line through the reference origin give a centred mass distribution whose inertia matrix has a zero principal moment and is not invertible, and a rotation of the model about that line has zero rotational kinetic energy and zero angular momentum about the centre of mass. The item refutes only the claim that every positive-mass rigid-material model has positive definite inertia; it asserts no measured value and no failure of the model's other statements, which carry the degeneracy caveat.

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, January 2015 printing), Section 3.2, Eq. (3.22) and the equality-case discussion, printed page 52 (PDF page 58): the inertia quadratic form vanishes precisely when all the mass lies on a line through the centre of mass

K. K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Part CM: Classical Mechanics (title page last edited September 1, 2026), Chapter 4 Section 4.4, chapter pages 8-11 (PDF pages 62-65): the warning that degenerate mass distributions require care with the inertia tensor, in the free symmetric-top discussion

G. J. Sussman and J. Wisdom, Structure and Interpretation of Classical Mechanics, 2nd ed. (MIT Press, 2014), Sections 2.3-2.5: the moment of inertia about an axis and the principal moments of discrete mass distributions, including the case of collinear mass

items.title: The Euler-angle pole: a degenerate parametrization of $SO(3)$ while the physical orientation remains regular
items.statement:
Let $R_z,R_y$ be the coordinate rotation matrices of
[[lem-cm-coordinate-rotation-matrices]] and consider the formula of the
Euler-angle parametrization of
[[def-cm-euler-angle-parametrization-and-heavy-top-system]],
$$\Phi:\mathbb R^3\longrightarrow M_3(\mathbb R),\qquad \Phi(\alpha,\beta,\gamma):=R_z(\alpha)R_y(\beta)R_z(\gamma),$$
here read on the whole parameter space $\mathbb R^3$ (the definition restricts
its chart domain to $\beta\in(0,\pi)$). Then:

1. $\Phi(\alpha,0,\gamma)=R_z(\alpha+\gamma)$: at the **pole** $\beta=0$ the
   value depends only on the sum $\alpha+\gamma$, and for every real $s$
   $$\Phi(\alpha+s,0,\gamma-s)=\Phi(\alpha,0,\gamma);$$
   hence $\Phi$ is not injective on any neighbourhood of a pole point.
2. the partial derivatives at a pole point satisfy
   $$\partial_\alpha\Phi(\alpha,0,\gamma)=\partial_\gamma\Phi(\alpha,0,\gamma)=[e_3]_\times R_z(\alpha+\gamma),$$
   so the Jacobian matrix has two identical columns, its rank is at most $2$,
   and it is not invertible; consequently $\Phi$ has no differentiable local
   inverse at any pole point;
3. along a smooth curve $t\mapsto(\alpha(t),\beta(t),\gamma(t))$ through a
   pole point ($\beta(0)=0$) the body angular velocity of the resulting
   rotation path is
   $$\omega(0)=(\alpha'(0)+\gamma'(0))\,e_3+\beta'(0)\,R_z(-\gamma(0))e_2,$$
   so the individual rates $\alpha'$ and $\gamma'$ enter only through their
   sum: the triples of rates $(\alpha',\beta',\gamma')$ and
   $(\alpha'+s,\beta',\gamma'-s)$ produce the same angular velocity, and the
   rate map of the parametrization is not injective at the pole;
4. nevertheless the orientation path
   $$R:\mathbb R\longrightarrow SO(3),\qquad R(t):=R_y(t),$$
   of a rigid-material model passes through the pole orientation
   $R(0)=I_3=\Phi(0,0,0)$, is of class $C^\infty$, and has the constant body
   angular velocity $e_2$; the singularity of clause 2 is a property of the
   parametrization, not of the orientation or of the angular velocity.
items.physical_scope: A worked example about the Euler-angle description of the orientation of the rigid-material model branch of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: at the pole $\beta=0$ the parametrization is non-injective and its derivative has rank at most two, so it is not a chart there, and the map from Euler-angle rates to the body angular velocity loses injectivity; meanwhile the orientation path $R(t)=R_y(t)$ passes through the pole orientation with constant angular velocity $e_2$ and is perfectly regular. The item asserts no dynamics, no measurement and no claim that the orientation of a concrete body has been recorded.

references.title: G. J. Sussman and J. Wisdom, Structure and Interpretation of Classical Mechanics, 2nd ed. (MIT Press, 2014), Section 2.7 and Section 2.8.1: the Euler-angle parametrization, the chart's exclusion of the poles $\sin\theta=0$, and the $ABC\sin^{2}\theta$ Hessian determinant of the coordinate transformation

K. K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Part CM: Classical Mechanics (title page last edited September 1, 2026), Chapter 4 Sections 4.5-4.6, chapter pages 15-22 (PDF pages 69-76): Euler angles as local coordinates and the warning that the angular-velocity components are not globally coordinate derivatives

D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, January 2015 printing), Section 3.5, printed pages 62-65 (PDF pages 68-71): the three ordered rotations defining the Euler angles and the caution about the convention and the local character of the angles

items.title: Parallel-axis check for the equilateral-triangle model: inertia tensor about a vertex computed two ways
items.statement:
Adopt the equilateral-triangle rigid-material model of
[[ex-cm10-equilateral-triangle-rotational-inertia]]: three equal point masses
$m_0>0$ at $x_k=a(\cos\frac{2\pi k}{3},\sin\frac{2\pi k}{3},0)$, $k=0,1,2$, with
total mass $m=3m_0$, body inertia matrix
$I=\mathrm{diag}(\frac{3m_0a^{2}}{2},\frac{3m_0a^{2}}{2},3m_0a^{2})$ and
reference coordinates centred at the origin. Then:

1. for every motion of the model and every spatial point $p$, the inertia
   tensor of the model about $p$ satisfies the **spatial parallel-axis form**
   $$I(t,p)=I(t)+m\Bigl(\lVert p-c(t)\rVert_2^{2}I_3-(p-c(t))(p-c(t))^{\mathsf T}\Bigr);$$
2. in the reference placement $(c,R)=(0,I_3)$, the inertia tensor about the
   vertex $p=ae_1$ is
   $$I(0,ae_1)=\mathrm{diag}\Bigl(\frac{3m_0a^{2}}{2},\ \frac{9m_0a^{2}}{2},\ 6m_0a^{2}\Bigr);$$
3. the same matrix is obtained by the direct finite sum over the three
   material points, confirming the identity of clause 1 on this data;
4. the moment of inertia about the axis through the vertex $ae_1$ in
   direction $e_3$ equals $6m_0a^{2}$, while the moment about the parallel
   central axis is $3m_0a^{2}$; their difference is $ma^{2}$, in agreement
   with the axis-shift form of the theorem.
items.physical_scope: A worked instance of the parallel-axis theorem in the rigid-material model branch of [[post-cm10-rigid-material]]: for the equilateral-triangle model of the companion example, the inertia tensor of the model about a vertex is computed from the supplier's shifted-point formula and independently from the finite sum defining it, and the two agree; the axis moment about the vertex axis is compared with the central axis moment. The item asserts no measured inertia and no concrete physical body.

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, January 2015 printing), Section 3.2.1, Eqs. (3.25)-(3.26), printed pages 52-53 (PDF pages 58-59): the inertia tensor about a displaced point and the parallel-axis relation

K. K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Part CM: Classical Mechanics (title page last edited September 1, 2026), Chapter 4 Section 4.2, Eqs. (4.27)-(4.29), chapter pages 6-7 (PDF pages 60-61): the axis-shift theorem and its use in computed examples
I. Stewart, Advanced Classical Mechanics (MIT 8.09/8.309 Fall 2014 course text), Chapter 2 Section 2.3, printed pages 37-41 (PDF pages 40-44): the parallel-axis derivation for the inertia tensor
